title: In most car engines, each cylinder burns fuel once every two turns
body: A four-stroke engine’s piston makes four trips per cycle: down to draw in fuel and air (intake), up to squeeze it (compression), down again as it burns (power), and up to push the burnt gas out (exhaust). Each stroke is half a turn of the crankshaft, so one cycle takes two turns, and only the power stroke does work. The connecting rod and crank turn the piston’s up-and-down motion into rotation, while a camshaft turning at half the crankshaft’s speed opens each valve once per cycle. In a petrol engine a spark plug ignites the mixture; a diesel relies on the heat of compression instead.

slides.alt: Animated blueprint, a simplified cutaway of one petrol-engine cylinder: crank and connecting rod drive the piston, cams open the valves. Over two crank turns the gas goes from fresh mixture to compressed, burning after the spark, then exhaust, as a counter tracks the four strokes.

slides.prompt: The valves are worked by a camshaft that turns at exactly half the crankshaft’s speed. Why half?
slides.answer: Each valve opens once per cycle, and a cycle takes two crank turns.
slides.detail: One turn of the camshaft per cycle lets each cam push its valve open once, during the right part of the intake or exhaust stroke.

slides.heading: Why squeeze it first?
slides.text: Étienne Lenoir’s gas engine of 1860 burned its fuel without compressing it and turned only about 4% of the fuel’s energy into work. Otto’s engine of 1876 compressed the mixture before igniting it, for far higher efficiency than any engine before it.

slides.heading: The spark comes early
slides.text: At low engine speeds, the spark fires close to the top of the compression stroke. At higher revs it fires earlier: the flame doesn’t burn any faster, so it needs a head start before the power stroke begins.

slides.heading: Not quite on the dot
slides.text: In the animation the valves open and close exactly at the top and bottom of each stroke. Real valves open a little early and close a little late, and at the end of the exhaust stroke both are briefly open at once, which helps the outgoing gas draw in the fresh charge.

slides.heading: Petrol engine or diesel?

items.text: Lit by the heat of compression
Fuel rated by its octane number
Fuel rated by its cetane number
Often helped by a glow plug on cold starts

slides.explanation: A petrol engine ignites its mixture with a timed spark. A diesel squeezes air until it is hot enough to ignite the fuel, so it needs no spark plug.
